name: Prize crossword No 28,673
preamble: Several solutions (not further defined) are of a kind

clue.text: Imitative play every other playroom day

indicators.note: taking every other one means keeping one, skipping one, and so on along the run of letters

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on of these two words run together

explanation.surface: A child's pretend game, played on alternate days in the playroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words run together as one string, PLAYROOMDAY, before the alternate letters are taken, starting with the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A parody is a comic piece that mimics another work's style, so it is a dramatic or written imitation.

clue.text: Turns boat east, overtaken by larger vessel

indicators.note: something overtaken is caught and swallowed up, so it ends up inside the other part

blocks.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat
E is the compass abbreviation
SS stands for steamship, bigger than a ketch

explanation.surface: A small boat swings east and is overhauled by a bigger ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns' reads like a verb about the boat's course, but it is the definition, in its theatrical sense: comic turns or acts.
explanation.definitionFit: In variety theatre a turn is a short performance, and short comic scenes in a revue are sketches.

clue.text: Horrible ogre grabs unnamed girl

indicators.note: something horrible is ugly and misshapen, so these letters are twisted into a new order
to grab is to seize and hold, so one part holds the other inside it
N is the abbreviation for name, so being without a name means losing that letter

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Ann is a girl's name; dropping one N leaves AN

explanation.surface: A nasty monster snatches a nameless girl, like a fairy-tale villain.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says some answers are of one kind, here fruit, with no definition given. Ann loses the N for 'name' and sits inside the rearranged monster.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble's shared kind is fruit, and the orange is a familiar citrus fruit from that category.

clue.text: Fruit exchanged in the event!

indicators.note: what is changed is altered into a different form, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word splits as 'ex' plus 'changed'; the front part, a former partner, is kept as letters

explanation.surface: Fruit gets swapped about at some occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'exchanged' as 'ex-changed': its first two letters are added to the fodder and the rest is the anagram signal. The exclamation mark flags the cheeky split.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixture is a scheduled sporting match or meeting, an event fixed in the calendar.

clue.text: One who puts an oar in noisily

indicators.note: something done noisily is heard rather than seen, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.clueFragment: One who puts an oar in
blocks.note: to put your oar in is to interfere, so this is a busybody

explanation.surface: A busybody who loudly sticks their oar into other people's business.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'put your oar in' is an idiom for interfering. The busybody's name is said the same as a fruit, which the preamble leaves undefined.
explanation.definitionFit: The medlar is a small brown fruit of the rose family, eaten when half-rotten, so it fits the preamble's shared kind.

clue.text: One consumed by passions seen regularly after meat or sugar

definitions.text: seen regularly after meat or sugar

indicators.note: what is consumed is swallowed, so it ends up inside the other part

blocks.note: loves are passions; this is the front of that word
a means one
the rest of the same word, which wraps round the inserted letter

explanation.surface: Someone eaten up by desire, glimpsed now and then after a meal of meat or sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen regularly' looks like an alternate-letters signal, but it belongs to the definition: the answer is a word often found after 'meat' or 'sugar'.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat loaves and sugar loaves are common compounds, so this plural noun regularly follows those words.

clue.text: Boatman's work may bear this

blocks.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, someone who works on boats
hard work is said to bear fruit when it pays off

explanation.surface: Boatman, the setter, hopes this puzzle will pay off for the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is this puzzle's setter, so the clue reads as him talking about his own work. Jack is old slang for a sailor; the fruit itself goes undefined, per the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackfruit is a huge tropical fruit from South Asia, one of the fruits the preamble groups together.

clue.text: Lemon crush, sometimes topped with water

indicators.note: something crushed is squashed out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A lemon squash drink, now and then diluted with water poured on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topped with water' means the word is sometimes preceded by 'water', as in watermelon; in an across entry the front is the top-left.
explanation.definitionFit: Watermelon is a common fruit name, so this word is the one that often carries 'water' in front.

clue.text: Skill catching fish? It's having good luck

indicators.note: to catch is to trap and hold, so one part goes inside the other

blocks.note: a forte is someone's strong point
tuna is a large sea fish

explanation.surface: An angler's talent for landing fish: is it really just being lucky?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the wordplay; 'It's' links it to the definition that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortunate is a straightforward synonym for lucky, describing someone favoured by chance.

clue.text: Nothing wrong about  …

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: O looks like zero
evil is wrongdoing

explanation.surface: Nothing is wrong about it, the ellipsis says, trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to the next clue but plays no part in the wordplay. The fruit is undefined, as the preamble allows.
explanation.definitionFit: The olive is the small oily stone fruit of the Mediterranean olive tree, matching the preamble's shared kind.

clue.text: The Listener goes under quietly

indicators.note: in a down entry, going under means being placed lower, so this part follows the other

blocks.note: p, piano, is the musical direction to play quietly
the ear is the organ that listens

explanation.surface: The Listener, a famously hard crossword, is quietly being dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: The Listener is a notoriously difficult Times crossword, which makes the surface read as crossword gossip; here it is just an ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The pear is a common orchard fruit, one of the fruits the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: …  thoroughly cheeky crossword setting

indicators.note: a setting is a mount that holds a stone, and the words across hold the answer within them

blocks.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a very cheeky bit of crossword setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossword setting' reads as composing puzzles, a nod to the setter, but 'setting' is the signal that the letters are held within.
explanation.definitionFit: The lychee is a small sweet Chinese fruit with a rough red skin, one of the preamble's group.

clue.text: Seeds at Wimbledon are embarrassingly volatile, but not lamebrain characters

indicators.note: volatile means unstable and liable to change, so the letters do not keep their order
taking something but not something else means subtracting the second from the first

blocks.note: taken as written
the letters of this word are struck out of the longer string

explanation.surface: Top-seeded players at Wimbledon are prone to awkward outbursts, though not stupid ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove each letter of LAMEBRAIN from ARE EMBARRASSINGLY, leaving ARERSSGY, then rearrange. 'Seeds' suggests tennis seeds, but the courts are sown with this grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Wimbledon's grass courts are sown with perennial ryegrass, so the seed sown there is this plant.

clue.text: See 17
See 16
Busted split up finally to produce electronic dance music

indicators.note: something split is broken apart, so its letters can be reassembled differently
finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A band that has busted up finally reinvents itself as an electronic act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busted' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'split' does the rearranging. Busted was also a British pop band that split up.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubstep is a genre of bass-heavy electronic music that emerged in South London around 2000.

clue.text: Wandering nomads

indicators.note: wandering things stray from their path, so the letters drift out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Nomadic peoples roaming from place to place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering' seems to describe the nomads, but it signals the rearrangement. The fruit is undefined, per the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: The damson is a small dark plum, one of the fruits the preamble groups without definition.

clue.text: Suppress literary gossip

blocks.note: to ban is to forbid or suppress
ana is a collection of anecdotes or table talk about a writer

explanation.surface: Keep the scandal about authors quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: ANA is an old word for a collection of sayings or gossip about someone, as in the suffix of Victoriana; it is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The banana is a long curved tropical fruit, which belongs to the preamble's undefined kind.

clue.text: Solver reported on river vessel

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its sound is what counts
in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so this part comes first

blocks.note: the clue addresses the solver as you; the word for a female sheep is said the same
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A solver files a report from aboard a river boat.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the solver is 'you'. 'river vessel' looks like a boat, but the river gives a letter and 'vessel' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug with a wide spout, a container for water; vessel covers any container for liquid.

clue.text: Here it is, in b*** downpour

indicators.note: a piece placed in another goes inside its letters

blocks.note: the starred-out swear word is just its first letter
rain is a downpour
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grumble about the weather: here we are, in the bloody rain again.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian is a British paper, so 'Here' is where setter and solver are. The censored 'b***' (bloody) is a joke about British swearing and British rain.
explanation.definitionFit: For a setter of a British newspaper, the place called here is the country where it is published.

clue.text: River in Devon at its source

indicators.note: a source is where a stream starts, so only the opening letter is used

blocks.note: the Tamar forms the border between Devon and Cornwall
taken as written
the first letter of the county

explanation.surface: A river in Devon, near the point where it rises.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a river in Devon and the River Tamar is one, on the Devon-Cornwall border; but 'in' is literal letters, not location.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamarind is the sour pod fruit of a tropical tree, used in cooking, one of the preamble's group.

clue.text: Love the Lakes? Love one of the Moors

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
taken as written
L is lake, doubled for the plural
the same zero score again

explanation.surface: Do you love the Lake District, or would you rather love the Yorkshire Moors?
explanation.walkthrough: The Lakes and the Moors read as English landscapes. 'the Moors' is the definition's trap: here a Moor is a North African, not moorland.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Othello is subtitled the Moor of Venice, so the title character is a famous Moor.

clue.text: It's intended to remind one of time shortly before Spirit Time

indicators.note: coming before means being placed earlier in the line, so this part leads

blocks.note: mo is a short way of saying moment
a numen is a presiding spirit or divinity
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A device meant to remind someone that Spirit Time is nearly here.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMEN, a Latin word for a local deity, is the uncommon piece. 'time' and 'Time' do different jobs: one shortened word, one abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A monument is a statue or structure built to commemorate, which is exactly a reminder of a person or event.

clue.text: Not allowing U-turns or a change in direction when reversing

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so this part is read the other way

blocks.note: a means one
a yaw is a swing off course by a ship or aircraft

explanation.surface: A traffic sign: no U-turns, no changing direction while you back up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue sounds like a road rule. The reversing applies only to the change in direction, not to the 'a' before it.
explanation.definitionFit: On a one-way street traffic may flow in a single direction only, so turning round to go back is barred.

clue.text: Naked guy, once eager and free

indicators.note: naked means stripped of clothes, so each word loses its outer letters

blocks.note: the word without its outside letters
the word without its outside letters
the word without its outside letters

explanation.surface: A naked man, once keen and unrestrained, as in a racy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' applies to all three following words, stripping the first and last letter from each.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncage an animal is to let it out of its cage, so it is a specific way to set something at liberty.

clue.text: It originates in gonads and might engage the egg

definitions.text: It originates in gonads and might engage the egg

indicators.note: where something originates is its starting point, so the first letters are used

blocks.clueFragment: gonads and might engage the egg
blocks.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A biology lesson on reproductive cells and fertilisation.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the initials of the last six words spell the answer, and the sentence describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamete is a sex cell made in the testes or ovaries; a sperm gamete fuses with the egg in fertilisation.

clue.text: Complains, replacing one with another one

indicators.note: replacing means swapping out one letter and putting a different one in its spot

blocks.note: to gripe is to grumble
I is the Roman numeral one, which is taken out
a also means one, and it goes in

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about one thing being swapped for another.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'one' and 'another one' stand for a single letter meaning one: Roman I out, the article A in.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapes are the berries of the vine, eaten fresh or made into wine, and belong to the preamble's fruit set.

clue.text: Could be felt inside, as well

indicators.note: something inside is enclosed by the other part

blocks.note: too means as well
a mat might be made of felt

explanation.surface: Something might be sensed within you, too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'felt' looks like the past of 'feel', but it is the fabric; a mat is one thing it could be. The fruit itself is undefined, per the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the tomato is a berry, a fruit, though cooks treat it as a vegetable, so it joins the preamble's group.

clue.text: Penny apiece

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny in British money
apiece means each

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a price tag, a penny each, which suits a fruit stall. The fruit itself is left undefined, as the preamble says.
explanation.definitionFit: The peach is a soft downy stone fruit, one of the fruits the preamble leaves undefined in this puzzle.

clue.text: Stars Meg and Sarah naughtily snatch a kiss

indicators.note: acting naughtily means misbehaving, so the letters do not stay in line
to snatch is to grab and hold, so one part is gripped inside the other

blocks.note: the two names, without the joining word
X is the kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Two film stars named Meg and Sarah cheekily steal a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' sounds like celebrities, and the names support that, but it is the definition: six-pointed star shapes. 'and' simply joins the names.
explanation.definitionFit: A hexagram is a six-pointed figure made from two overlapping triangles, such as the Star of David.

clue.text: Cycling comic Dave, missing start of ride

indicators.note: cycling goes round and round, so letters move from one end of the word to the other
what is missing is absent, so that letter is taken away
the start of a word is its opening letter, which is the one removed

blocks.note: Dave Gorman is a British stand-up comedian and TV presenter
the first letter, which is dropped

explanation.surface: A comedian named Dave out on his bike, missing the start of the ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Dave Gorman is a British comedian. Remove R to get GOMAN, then move GO from the front to the back. 'Cycling' sounds like the bike ride but moves letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The mango is a sweet tropical stone fruit, one of the fruits the preamble groups together without definition.

clue.text: Liverpool's terminus follows a three-way interchange

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this part is placed second
a terminus is the end of a line, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the city's name
ternate means arranged in threes, a botanical word

explanation.surface: At a three-way rail junction, the Liverpool line's final stop comes next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terminus' and 'interchange' both sound like railway terms. TERNATE describes leaves set in threes. 'interchange' is a verb here: to swap turns.
explanation.definitionFit: To alternate is to take turns or switch back and forth, so it means to interchange in succession.
